accepted.question_text: For a symmetric convex body, must the two points that are farthest apart when distance is measured along the surface of the body be opposite, or antipodal, points of that body? The page notes that this question appears to remain open even for rectangular boxes.

evidence.quote:
Jim Propp asks whether the two farthest apart points,
as measured by surface distance, on a symmetric convex body
must be opposite each other on the body.
Apparently this is open even for rectangular boxes.

accepted.question_text: Does every convex polytope admit a triangulation in which the degree of each vertex, or alternatively the degree of each edge, is bounded either by a constant or by a polylogarithmic bound?

evidence.quote:
Pankaj Agarwal and Sandeep Sen ask for triangulations of convex polytopes
in which the vertex or edge degree is bounded by a constant or polylog.

accepted.question_text: Given six points in the Euclidean plane together with a maximum, rather than minimum, matching on those points, does there exist a point whose distance from every matched edge is at most a universal constant times the length of that edge?

evidence.quote:
Andy Fingerhut asks, given a maximum (not minimum) matching of six
points in the Euclidean plane, whether there is a center point
close to all matched edges (within distance a constant times the length
of the edge).  If so, it could be extended to more points via Helly's theorem.
Apparently this is related to communication network design.
I include a response I sent with a proof (of a constant worse than the
one he wanted, but generalizing as well to bipartite matching).

accepted.question_text: How many colors are necessary to color the Euclidean plane so that no two points at distance exactly one from each other receive the same color? In other words, what is the chromatic number of the unit-distance graph of the plane?

evidence.quote:
Gordon Royle and Ilan Vardi summarize what's known about
the famous open problem of how many colors are needed to color
the plane so that no two points at a unit distance apart get the same color.

accepted.question_text: Given a finite set of points in the plane and a fixed rectangle shape, how well can one approximate the minimum number of congruent copies of that rectangle needed to cover all of the points? The page states that exact optimization is NP-hard and highlights the approximability question as the open part.

evidence.quote:
Stan Shebs discusses the problem of finding a minimum number of
copies of a given rectangle that will cover all points in some set,
and mentions an application to a computer strategy game.
This is NP-hard, but I don't know how easy it is to approximate;
most related work I know of is on optimizing the rectangle size for a cover
by a fixed number of rectangles.

accepted.question_text: Can a three-dimensional cube be partitioned into tetrahedra that are pairwise congruent and have disjoint interiors?

evidence.quote: Can one divide a cube into congruent and disjoint tetrahedra?

accepted.question_text: If the congruence requirement is dropped, how many simplices are needed to triangulate a hypercube in higher dimensions?

evidence.quote:
And without the congruence assumption,
how many higher dimensional simplices are needed to triangulate a hypercube?

accepted.question_text: Does the hyperbolic plane admit an isometric immersion into four-dimensional Euclidean space R^4?

evidence.quote:
D. Rusin summarizes what's known; the existence of an isometric
immersion into R4 is apparently open.

accepted.question_text: Do there exist seven points in the Euclidean plane in general position, meaning that no three are collinear and no four lie on a common circle, such that every pairwise distance between the seven points is an integer?

evidence.quote:
Robert Israel gives a nice proof (originally due to Erdös) of the
fact that,
in any non-colinear planar point set in which all distances
are integers, there are only finitely many points.
Infinite sets of points with rational distances are known,
from which arbitrarily large finite sets of points with integer
distances can be constructed; however it is open whether there are even
seven points at integer distances in general position
(no three in a line and no four on a circle).

accepted.question_text: If a polygon has perfectly reflecting sides and contains a point source of light, must every point of the polygon be illuminated by some direct or reflected light ray from that source?

evidence.quote:
A summary by Christine Piatko of the old open problem of, given
a polygon in which all sides are perfect mirrors, and a point source
of light, whether the entire polygon will be lit up.
The answer is no if smooth curves are allowed.

accepted.question_text: Let P be the polyomino obtained from a 3 by 6 rectangle by removing a 2 by 2 bite. Although P can tile some larger rectangle, is it possible for P to tile a rectangle using an odd number of congruent copies of P?

evidence.quote:
Michael Reid shows that a 3x6 rectangle with a 2x2
bite removed can tile a (much larger) rectangle.
It is open whether it can do this using an odd number of copies.

accepted.question_text: One tetrahedron can be entirely contained inside another tetrahedron while having a larger total edge length. How large can this excess be, or equivalently how much larger can the sum of the contained tetrahedron's edge lengths be than the sum of the containing tetrahedron's edge lengths?

evidence.quote:
One tetrahedron can be entirely contained in
another, and yet have a larger sum of edge lengths. But how much larger?

accepted.question_text: Suppose a family of unit disks moves in such a way that every pairwise distance between disk centers decreases. Must the area of the union of the disks also decrease?

evidence.quote:
If unit disks move so their pairwise distances all
decrease, does the area of their union also decrease?

accepted.question_text: If a polytope has n faces, is it always true that any two of its vertices can be connected in the graph of the polytope by a path of O(n) edges?
accepted.context_brief: linear diameter conjecture for polytope graphs

evidence.quote:
A famous open conjecture in polyhedral
combinatorics (with applications to e.g. the simplex method in linear
programming) states that any two vertices of an n-face polytope are
linked by a chain of O(n) edges.  This paper gives the weaker bound
O(nlog d).

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a triangle for which all three side lengths, all three medians, all three altitudes, and the area are rational numbers?

evidence.quote:
This well known problem asks whether there exists a triangle with
the side lengths, medians, altitudes, and area all rational numbers.
Randall Rathbun provides some "near misses" -- triangles in which
most but not all of these quantities are irrational.

accepted.question_text: Does every Jordan curve in the plane contain four points that are the vertices of a square?

evidence.quote:
Various people discuss the open problem of whether any Jordan curve
in the plane contains four points forming the vertices of a square,
and the related but not open problem of how to place
a square table level on a hilltop.

accepted.question_text: Is there an efficient algorithm on the Turing-machine model for comparing a sum of square roots of integers with an integer, or with another similar sum of square roots of integers?

evidence.quote:
A major bottleneck
in proving NP-completeness for geometric problems is a mismatch between
the real-number and Turing machine models of computation: one is good
for geometric algorithms but bad for reductions, and the other vice
versa.  Specifically, it is not known on Turing machines how to quickly
compare a sum of distances (square roots of integers) with an integer or
other similar sums, so even (decision versions of) easy problems such as
the minimum spanning tree are not known to be in NP.  
Joe O'Rourke
discusses an approach to this problem based on bounding the smallest
difference between two such sums, so that one could know how precise an
approximation to compute.

accepted.question_text: For every positive integer k, consider the rectangle of side lengths 1/k and 1/(k+1). Since the total area of all of these rectangles is 1, is it possible to pack the entire infinite family together to tile a unit square exactly?
accepted.context_brief: tiling the unit square with harmonic rectangles

evidence.quote:
Erich Friedman
shows that the 5/6 by 5/6 square can always be tiled with 1/(k+1) by
1/(k+1) squares.
Will all the 1/k by 1/(k+1) rectangles, for k>0,
fit together in a unit square?
Note that the sum of the rectangle areas is 1. 
Marc Paulhus can fit them into
a square of side 1.000000001.

accepted.question_text: Find a guaranteed lower-bound function t(n) such that every convex polygon with n vertices has a triangulation containing at least t(n) triangles of pairwise distinct areas.

evidence.quote:
Eddie Grove asks for a function t(n) such that any n-vertex convex polygon
has a triangulation with at least t(n) distinct triangle areas,
and also discusses a special case in which the vertices are points in a
lattice.

accepted.question_text: Is every convex polyhedron edge-unfoldable, meaning that one can cut along edges of the polyhedron so that its boundary unfolds into a single simple planar polygon without self-overlap?

evidence.quote:
Catherine Schevon discusses whether it is always possible
to cut a convex polyhedron's edges so its boundary unfolds into a simple
planar polygon.
